sources.text:
A scheduler chooses which ready job receives the processor. Turnaround time equals completion time minus arrival time. Response time equals the first time a job runs minus its arrival time. These metrics measure different things: early access to a processor does not necessarily imply early completion. First-come, first-served runs jobs in arrival order without preempting them. Shortest Job First selects the shortest available job and is non-preemptive. Shortest Time-to-Completion First is preemptive and selects the job with the least remaining processing time. Comparisons involving these shortest-job policies must state how execution lengths are known.

Round Robin rotates through a ready queue, running each selected job for at most one time slice before moving an unfinished job to the back. Shorter slices can improve initial responsiveness but increase the frequency of context switches. Larger slices amortize switching costs but can lengthen waits before a different job first runs. Neither a smaller average response time nor a smaller switching fraction alone establishes that a policy is best for every objective.

A multi-level feedback queue, or MLFQ, uses observed execution behavior instead of requiring exact future job lengths. Jobs in higher-priority queues run before lower-priority jobs; equal-priority jobs can share service by Round Robin. New jobs begin at high priority, and consuming the allowed CPU allotment causes demotion. Accounting for total consumed allotment prevents a job from retaining high priority indefinitely merely by yielding just before each slice ends. Periodic priority boosts can help jobs otherwise left waiting at low priority. Queue levels, slice lengths, allotments, and boost intervals are policy parameters, not universal constants.

This fixture adds an explicit scheduling model for exercises. It is authored example scaffolding rather than text copied from a textbook. Unless a question states otherwise, there is one processor, jobs are independent, and each job consists of one CPU burst with no I/O. Arrival times and required CPU service are provided. The processor never serves two jobs simultaneously. Time spent switching is not CPU service delivered to any job. A job that finishes before its slice ends does not use the remaining slice. If a job arrives at exactly a slice boundary, the question must say whether that arrival is enqueued before or after the preempted job. Ties must be resolved by an explicit rule, such as alphabetical job names.

A question that includes switching overhead must define when that overhead applies: for example, only when moving between different jobs, with no initial dispatch charge. It must also state whether arrivals can occur while switching and how they enter the queue. Questions that ignore overhead must say so. These conventions make a timeline reproducible and prevent a numeric answer from depending on unstated simulator behavior.

A comparison can report each job's first-run and completion times, then compute the requested averages. A design recommendation also needs an objective and constraints, such as a maximum response time, a switching budget, or a fairness requirement. A policy can satisfy one constraint while losing on another metric. Choosing a scheduler should therefore follow the stated workload and requirements. Hypothetical burst lengths and budgets introduced in an exercise are not measured workload traces, and labels assigned by the generator are not empirical student difficulty measurements.

learning_objectives: Compute execution timelines and process metrics under explicit scheduling rules.

sections.heading: Scheduling metrics and conventions
sections.text: Processes are independent, have a single CPU burst and no I/O, on one processor with integer abstract time units. The listed burst lengths are known inputs supplied for this exercise, not predictions of a real workload. A completed process stops immediately without consuming the unused part of its quantum; any waiver of the following switching cost is a separate scenario rule. Simultaneous arrivals use lexicographic process ID order. Initial dispatch, dispatch after idle, and same-process continuation are free. Response time = first start − arrival; turnaround time = completion − arrival. Makespan is final completion measured from t=0, including all idle and switching time. Switch count includes adjacent different-process transitions, even free transitions, and excludes initial/after-idle dispatch. Timeline intervals are half-open [start, end); consecutive same-process runs are merged unless separated by switching or idle.

expected_steps: Order execution and switching intervals using the stated rules.
Compute process metrics and exact averages from first starts and completions.
Check service conservation and the requested state or constraint judgments.

questions.stem:
Processes are independent, have a single CPU burst and no I/O, on one processor with integer abstract time units. The listed burst lengths are known inputs supplied for this exercise, not predictions of a real workload. A completed process stops immediately without consuming the unused part of its quantum; any waiver of the following switching cost is a separate scenario rule. Simultaneous arrivals use lexicographic process ID order. Initial dispatch, dispatch after idle, and same-process continuation are free. Response time = first start − arrival; turnaround time = completion − arrival. Makespan is final completion measured from t=0, including all idle and switching time. Switch count includes adjacent different-process transitions, even free transitions, and excludes initial/after-idle dispatch. Timeline intervals are half-open [start, end); consecutive same-process runs are merged unless separated by switching or idle.

Processes (arrival, burst):

P1: (0, 8)

P2: (0, 8)

P3: (0, 8)

P4: (2, 1)

P5: (0, 8)

rr_q2: RR; quantum q=2, different-process switching cost=1. Arrivals before a slice end are queued first; arrivals exactly at the slice end are queued before the unfinished process is requeued, while existing waiters keep their order. Select the next process before switching; arrivals during switching, including its end, are appended to the queue tail before the selected process starts. Waive the next different-process switching cost only when the previous process completed in its just-ended run slice and that slice was strictly shorter than a full quantum.

rr_q4: RR; quantum q=4, different-process switching cost=1. Arrivals before a slice end are queued first; arrivals exactly at the slice end are queued before the unfinished process is requeued, while existing waiters keep their order. Select the next process before switching; arrivals during switching, including its end, are appended to the queue tail before the selected process starts. Waive the next different-process switching cost only when the previous process completed in its just-ended run slice and that slice was strictly shorter than a full quantum.

stcf: STCF; switching cost is 0. At each integer time choose the arrived unfinished process with the smallest (remaining service, lexicographic process ID); a smaller ID can preempt the current process even when remaining service is equal.

For every scenario, give the complete timeline; each process’s first start, response, completion and turnaround; mean response, mean turnaround, switch count, total switching overhead and makespan. Use exact fractions for averages.

Among scenarios satisfying total switching overhead <= 8, minimize mean response time. Show every constraint check, report all tied optima, or state that no scenario is feasible.

Finally justify the selection using the computed metrics: explain the tradeoffs actually present between candidates, or state when metrics improve together or remain equal without an observed conflict. Explain why this result does not establish a policy that is optimal for every workload and objective.

rr_q2: service 33 + idle 0 + switching overhead 15 = makespan 48.
rr_q4: service 33 + idle 0 + switching overhead 7 = makespan 40.
stcf: service 33 + idle 0 + switching overhead 0 = makespan 33.

stcf: mean response time=51/5; mean turnaround time=17; total switching overhead=0; process switch count=5 → feasible under all stated constraints.
First filter to the feasible scenarios rr_q4, stcf, then minimize mean response time; all optimal scenarios are rr_q4, with objective value 48/5.
Comparing the four listed metrics in the lower-is-better direction reveals a real tradeoff among these candidates: rr_q2 has lower mean response time than rr_q4 (28/5 < 48/5), but higher total switching overhead (15 > 7). Evaluate the stated constraints and objective together rather than selecting on one metric alone.
This conclusion applies only to the supplied workload, finite candidates, objective and constraints. Lower mean response or lower switching overhead alone does not establish a universally optimal policy or quantum.

"fixture_cpu_scheduling_en", "text": "A scheduler chooses which ready job receives the processor. Turnaround time equals completion time minus arrival time. Response time equals the first time a job runs minus its arrival time. These metrics measure different things: early access to a processor does not necessarily imply early completion. First-come, first-served runs jobs in arrival order without preempting them. Shortest Job First selects the shortest available job and is non-preemptive. Shortest Time-to-Completion First is preemptive and selects the job with the least remaining processing time. Comparisons involving these shortest-job policies must state how execution lengths are known.

Round Robin rotates through a ready queue, running each selected job for at most one time slice before moving an unfinished job to the back. Shorter slices can improve initial responsiveness but increase the frequency of context switches. Larger slices amortize switching costs but can lengthen waits before a different job first runs. Neither a smaller average response time nor a smaller switching fraction alone establishes that a policy is best for every objective.

A multi-level feedback queue, or MLFQ, uses observed execution behavior instead of requiring exact future job lengths. Jobs in higher-priority queues run before lower-priority jobs; equal-priority jobs can share service by Round Robin. New jobs begin at high priority, and consuming the allowed CPU allotment causes demotion. Accounting for total consumed allotment prevents a job from retaining high priority indefinitely merely by yielding just before each slice ends. Periodic priority boosts can help jobs otherwise left waiting at low priority. Queue levels, slice lengths, allotments, and boost intervals are policy parameters, not universal constants.

This fixture adds an explicit scheduling model for exercises. It is authored example scaffolding rather than text copied from a textbook. Unless a question states otherwise, there is one processor, jobs are independent, and each job consists of one CPU burst with no I/O. Arrival times and required CPU service are provided. The processor never serves two jobs simultaneously. Time spent switching is not CPU service delivered to any job. A job that finishes before its slice ends does not use the remaining slice. If a job arrives at exactly a slice boundary, the question must say whether that arrival is enqueued before or after the preempted job. Ties must be resolved by an explicit rule, such as alphabetical job names.

A question that includes switching overhead must define when that overhead applies: for example, only when moving between different jobs, with no initial dispatch charge. It must also state whether arrivals can occur while switching and how they enter the queue. Questions that ignore overhead must say so. These conventions make a timeline reproducible and prevent a numeric answer from depending on unstated simulator behavior.

A comparison can report each job's first-run and completion times, then compute the requested averages. A design recommendation also needs an objective and constraints, such as a maximum response time, a switching budget, or a fairness requirement. A policy can satisfy one constraint while losing on another metric. Choosing a scheduler should therefore follow the stated workload and requirements. "fixture_cpu_scheduling_en", "text": "A scheduler chooses which ready job receives the processor. Turnaround time equals completion time minus arrival time. Response time equals the first time a job runs minus its arrival time. These metrics measure different things: early access to a processor does not necessarily imply early completion. First-come, first-served runs jobs in arrival order without preempting them. Shortest Job First selects the shortest available job and is non-preemptive. Shortest Time-to-Completion First is preemptive and selects the job with the least remaining processing time. Comparisons involving these shortest-job policies must state how execution lengths are known.

Round Robin rotates through a ready queue, running each selected job for at most one time slice before moving an unfinished job to the back. Shorter slices can improve initial responsiveness but increase the frequency of context switches. Larger slices amortize switching costs but can lengthen waits before a different job first runs. Neither a smaller average response time nor a smaller switching fraction alone establishes that a policy is best for every objective.

A multi-level feedback queue, or MLFQ, uses observed execution behavior instead of requiring exact future job lengths. Jobs in higher-priority queues run before lower-priority jobs; equal-priority jobs can share service by Round Robin. New jobs begin at high priority, and consuming the allowed CPU allotment causes demotion. Accounting for total consumed allotment prevents a job from retaining high priority indefinitely merely by yielding just before each slice ends. Periodic priority boosts can help jobs otherwise left waiting at low priority. Queue levels, slice lengths, allotments, and boost intervals are policy parameters, not universal constants.

These metrics measure different things: early access to a processor does not necessarily imply early completion. First-come, first-served runs jobs in arrival order without preempting them. Shortest Job First selects the shortest available job and is non-preemptive. Shortest Time-to-Completion First is preemptive and selects the job with the least remaining processing time. Comparisons involving these shortest-job policies must state how execution lengths are known.

Round Robin rotates through a ready queue, running each selected job for at most one time slice before moving an unfinished job to the back. Shorter slices can improve initial responsiveness but increase the frequency of context switches. Larger slices amortize switching costs but can lengthen waits before a different job first runs. Neither a smaller average response time nor a smaller switching fraction alone establishes that a policy is best for every objective.

A multi-level feedback queue, or MLFQ, uses observed execution behavior instead of requiring exact future job lengths. Turnaround time equals completion time minus arrival time. Response time equals the first time a job runs minus its arrival time. These metrics measure different things: early access to a processor does not necessarily imply early completion. First-come, first-served runs jobs in arrival order without preempting them. Shortest Job First selects the shortest available job and is non-preemptive. Shortest Time-to-Completion First is preemptive and selects the job with the least remaining processing time. Comparisons involving these shortest-job policies must state how execution lengths are known.

Round Robin rotates through a ready queue, running each selected job for at most one time slice before moving an unfinished job to the back. Shorter slices can improve initial responsiveness but increase the frequency of context switches. Larger slices amortize switching costs but can lengthen waits before a different job first runs. Neither a smaller average response time nor a smaller switching fraction alone establishes that a policy is best for every objective.

A multi-level feedback queue, or MLFQ, uses observed execution behavior instead of requiring exact future job lengths. Jobs in higher-priority queues run before lower-priority jobs; equal-priority jobs can share service by Round Robin. New jobs begin at high priority, and consuming the allowed CPU allotment causes demotion. Accounting for total consumed allotment prevents a job from retaining high priority indefinitely merely by yielding just before each slice ends. Periodic priority boosts can help jobs otherwise left waiting at low priority. Queue levels, slice lengths, allotments, and boost intervals are policy parameters, not universal constants.

function.name: mcp__teaching__cpu_schedule_v1
function.description:
Deterministic single-processor RR or STCF scheduling with independent, single-burst processes and no I/O. Times are integer abstract time units. Initial dispatch and dispatch after an idle interval are free. RR boundary=before/after orders arrivals exactly at a slice end before/after the unfinished process is requeued; earlier waiting processes keep their position. during_switch=tail appends switch-time arrivals to the queue; before_preempted inserts them immediately before the just-preempted process if it is still queued, otherwise at the tail. The next process is selected before switching, and arrivals through the switch end are enqueued before it starts. early_finish_free waives the next different-process switch cost only if the previous process completed in less than a full quantum. Same-process continuation is free. STCF supports zero switch cost only and chooses (remaining time, id), including id-based preemption on equal remaining times. Id comparison is Unicode lexicographic order. switch_count counts adjacent different-process transitions, including free early-finish transitions, but excludes initial/idle dispatch. makespan is final completion measured from time zero, including initial and intermediate idle intervals. Consecutive run intervals for the same process without an intervening switch/idle interval are merged.

function.name: mcp__teaching__cpu_schedule_v1
function.description:
Deterministic single-processor RR or STCF scheduling with independent, single-burst processes and no I/O. Times are integer abstract time units. Initial dispatch and dispatch after an idle interval are free. RR boundary=before/after orders arrivals exactly at a slice end before/after the unfinished process is requeued; earlier waiting processes keep their position. during_switch=tail appends switch-time arrivals to the queue; before_preempted inserts them immediately before the just-preempted process if it is still queued, otherwise at the tail. The next process is selected before switching, and arrivals through the switch end are enqueued before it starts. early_finish_free waives the next different-process switch cost only if the previous process completed in less than a full quantum. Same-process continuation is free. STCF supports zero switch cost only and chooses (remaining time, id), including id-based preemption on equal remaining times. Id comparison is Unicode lexicographic order. switch_count counts adjacent different-process transitions, including free early-finish transitions, but excludes initial/idle dispatch. makespan is final completion measured from time zero, including initial and intermediate idle intervals. Consecutive run intervals for the same process without an intervening switch/idle interval are merged.

sections.heading: Scheduling metrics and conventions
sections.text: Processes are independent, have a single CPU burst and no I/O, on one processor with integer abstract time units. The listed burst lengths are known inputs supplied for this exercise, not predictions of a real workload. A completed process stops immediately without consuming the unused part of its quantum; any waiver of the following switching cost is a separate scenario rule. Simultaneous arrivals use lexicographic process ID order. Initial dispatch, dispatch after idle, and same-process continuation are free. Response time = first start − arrival; turnaround time = completion − arrival. Makespan is final completion measured from t=0, including all idle and switching time. Switch count includes adjacent different-process transitions, even free transitions, and excludes initial/after-idle dispatch. Timeline intervals are half-open [start, end); consecutive same-process runs are merged unless separated by switching or idle.

expected_steps: Order execution and switching intervals using the stated rules.
Compute process metrics and exact averages from first starts and completions.
Check service conservation and the requested state or constraint judgments.

questions.stem:
Processes are independent, have a single CPU burst and no I/O, on one processor with integer abstract time units. The listed burst lengths are known inputs supplied for this exercise, not predictions of a real workload. A completed process stops immediately without consuming the unused part of its quantum; any waiver of the following switching cost is a separate scenario rule. Simultaneous arrivals use lexicographic process ID order. Initial dispatch, dispatch after idle, and same-process continuation are free. Response time = first start − arrival; turnaround time = completion − arrival. Makespan is final completion measured from t=0, including all idle and switching time. Switch count includes adjacent different-process transitions, even free transitions, and excludes initial/after-idle dispatch. Timeline intervals are half-open [start, end); consecutive same-process runs are merged unless separated by switching or idle.

Processes (arrival, burst):

P1: (0, 8)

P2: (0, 8)

P3: (0, 8)

P4: (2, 1)

P5: (0, 8)

rr_q2: RR; quantum q=2, different-process switching cost=1. Arrivals before a slice end are queued first; arrivals exactly at the slice end are queued before the unfinished process is requeued, while existing waiters keep their order. Select the next process before switching; arrivals during switching, including its end, are appended to the queue tail before the selected process starts. Waive the next different-process switching cost only when the previous process completed in its just-ended run slice and that slice was strictly shorter than a full quantum.

rr_q4: RR; quantum q=4, different-process switching cost=1. Arrivals before a slice end are queued first; arrivals exactly at the slice end are queued before the unfinished process is requeued, while existing waiters keep their order. Select the next process before switching; arrivals during switching, including its end, are appended to the queue tail before the selected process starts. Waive the next different-process switching cost only when the previous process completed in its just-ended run slice and that slice was strictly shorter than a full quantum.

stcf: STCF; switching cost is 0. At each integer time choose the arrived unfinished process with the smallest (remaining service, lexicographic process ID); a smaller ID can preempt the current process even when remaining service is equal.

For every scenario, give the complete timeline; each process’s first start, response, completion and turnaround; mean response, mean turnaround, switch count, total switching overhead and makespan. Use exact fractions for averages.

Among scenarios satisfying total switching overhead <= 8, minimize mean response time. Show every constraint check, report all tied optima, or state that no scenario is feasible.

Finally justify the selection using the computed metrics: explain the tradeoffs actually present between candidates, or state when metrics improve together or remain equal without an observed conflict. Explain why this result does not establish a policy that is optimal for every workload and objective.

Further analysis:
Using only the three frozen traces and metric blocks already given for rr_q2, rr_q4 and stcf (do not re-simulate, reorder or change any number), write a concise conceptual argument that does all of the following:

1. Define response time and turnaround time, then use one or more frozen values to show why a process can get its first run early yet finish late, or why two processes can share the same response while having very different turnarounds.
2. Report each process's first run and completion and the resulting mean response and mean turnaround for one RR scenario and for stcf, and name which process (for example the short job) drives each average.
3. Compare the candidates on mean response, mean turnaround, switch count and makespan, and state exactly where the rankings diverge (which scenario wins which metric).
4. Explain quantitatively how moving from q=2 to q=4 changed switch count, total switching overhead and mean response, and point to the specific stated rule that is visible in the traces (slice-boundary arrival, queue ordering during switching, ID/tie-breaking, or the early-finish switching waiver).
5. Check the constraint total switching overhead <= 8 for each scenario, apply the objective min mean response, name the winning scenario and its value, say whether any tie exists, and give one alternative constraint or objective under which the recommendation would change.
6. End by separating what these three runs establish from what they do not, and explain why no universally optimal policy or quantum follows from this example.

Keep the answer self-contained, refer to the original tables rather than reproducing the timelines, and use exact fractions for averages.

Optimal scenarios: rr_q4; mean response time=48/5.

Further analysis:
All numbers below are read from the supplied deterministic runs; nothing is re-simulated.

1) Definitions and the response/turnaround split. Response time = first start - arrival; turnaround time = completion - arrival. Response records only when a process first gets the processor; turnaround additionally contains every later wait, preemption and switching delay. Frozen evidence: P1 first starts at t=0 (response 0) in all three scenarios, yet its turnaround is 39 (rr_q2), 25 (rr_q4) and 9 (stcf). Same response, very different completion - early access does not imply early completion. Within one scenario the same contrast appears: P4 in rr_q2 has response 10 (first start 12, arrival 2) but turnaround 11 (completion 13), because its first start and its completion are separated by service and (for longer jobs) by repeated requeueing. Turnaround can never be smaller than response for the same process.

2) Per-process first run and completion, and the averages they drive. rr_q2: first starts 0, 3, 6, 12, 9 and completions 39, 42, 45, 13, 48 for P1..P5, so mean response = 28/5 and mean turnaround = 37. stcf: first starts 0, 9, 17, 2, 25 and completions 9, 17, 25, 3, 33, so mean response = 51/5 and mean turnaround = 17. (For completeness rr_q4: first starts 0, 5, 10, 20, 15; completions 25, 30, 35, 21, 40; mean response 48/5; mean turnaround 149/5.) Total service is 33 units in every scenario and idle time is 0, so makespan = 33 + total switching overhead: 48, 40 and 33 respectively - a conservation check that the traces satisfy.

3) Where the rankings diverge. Mean response favours rr_q2 (28/5 = 5.6) over rr_q4 (48/5 = 9.6) over stcf (51/5 = 10.2). Mean turnaround reverses almost completely: stcf 17, then rr_q4 149/5 = 29.8, then rr_q2 37. Switch count and overhead: stcf 5 switches / 0 overhead, rr_q4 8 / 7, rr_q2 16 / 15. Makespan: stcf 33, rr_q4 40, rr_q2 48. So the mean-response winner (rr_q2) is last on turnaround, switches and makespan, while stcf is first on three metrics but last on mean response. rr_q4 is never first, but is second on both response and turnaround. Concretely, stcf beats rr_q4 on mean response components only for the short job: P4's response is 0 under stcf versus 18 under rr_q4 (18 units better), while P3 is 7 units worse and P5 10 units worse; the per-process differences sum to 3, exactly the 3/5 gap in the means (51/5 - 48/5 = 3/5).

4) Slice length and switching overhead (q=2 vs q=4). Doubling the quantum halves the transitions, 16 to 8, and cuts overhead from 15 to 7, but mean response worsens from 28/5 to 48/5 (a rise of 4 units). The overhead is not simply half of the switch count twice over because each RR scenario has exactly one waived transition: P4 completes inside a run slice of length 1, strictly shorter than the full quantum (1 < 2 and 1 < 4), so the following P4 -> P1 transition is free, giving 16 - 1 = 15 and 8 - 1 = 7. Slice-boundary behaviour is visible too: P4 arrives exactly at t=2, the end of P1's first q=2 slice. The stated rule enqueues that arrival before requeueing the unfinished P1, producing the first-rotation order P2, P3, P5, P4, then P1 - the order the trace shows (P4 runs at 12, P1 at 13). Under q=4, P4 arrives during P1's slice [0,4) and is queued at arrival; the same relative position results, but P4's first start slips from 12 to 20 (response 10 to 18). The t=0 tie among the four equal-burst jobs is settled by the stated lexicographic ID rule in both RR queue order and, in stcf, by smallest (remaining service, ID).

5) Constraint, objective and recommendation. Constraint total switching overhead <= 8: rr_q2 has 15 (violates), rr_q4 has 7 (satisfies), stcf has 0 (satisfies). Feasible set = {rr_q4, stcf}. Objective min mean response: rr_q4 = 48/5 = 9.6 versus stcf = 51/5 = 10.2, margin 3/5. Recommendation: rr_q4, and it is the unique optimum - no tie. The choice is genuinely constraint-driven: if the budget were looser (for example overhead <= 15 or at most 16 switches), rr_q2 would become feasible and would then minimize mean response at 28/5; if the objective were mean turnaround or makespan instead of mean response, stcf would win (17 < 149/5 < 37; 33 < 40 < 48).

6) Scope. Facts: for this five-process instance with the burst lengths given as inputs, and under the stated free initial dispatch, free same-process continuation, half-open intervals, boundary-queueing and early-finish waiver rules, q=4 Round Robin is the feasible mean-response minimum and the three metrics rank as shown. Not established: that q=4, Round Robin or STCF is optimal for other workloads, other quantum values, or other objectives. A single trace family cannot support a universal policy claim, and a lower mean response or a lower switching fraction by itself does not decide which policy is best.
questions.explanation:
The listed burst lengths are known inputs supplied for this exercise. A completed process stops immediately without consuming the unused part of its quantum; whether the following switch is free must be determined separately from the scenario rules.
rr_q2: service 33 + idle 0 + switching overhead 15 = makespan 48.
rr_q4: service 33 + idle 0 + switching overhead 7 = makespan 40.
stcf: service 33 + idle 0 + switching overhead 0 = makespan 33.
rr_q2: mean response time=28/5; mean turnaround time=37; total switching overhead=15; process switch count=16 → infeasible; these required comparisons fail: total switching overhead 15 <= 8.
rr_q4: mean response time=48/5; mean turnaround time=149/5; total switching overhead=7; process switch count=8 → feasible under all stated constraints.
stcf: mean response time=51/5; mean turnaround time=17; total switching overhead=0; process switch count=5 → feasible under all stated constraints.
First filter to the feasible scenarios rr_q4, stcf, then minimize mean response time; all optimal scenarios are rr_q4, with objective value 48/5.
Comparing the four listed metrics in the lower-is-better direction reveals a real tradeoff among these candidates: rr_q2 has lower mean response time than rr_q4 (28/5 < 48/5), but higher total switching overhead (15 > 7). Evaluate the stated constraints and objective together rather than selecting on one metric alone.
This conclusion applies only to the supplied workload, finite candidates, objective and constraints. Lower mean response or lower switching overhead alone does not establish a universally optimal policy or quantum.

Further analysis:
Reading the supplement (audit notes).

What is fact and what is assumption. Everything in the answer is a fact about this frozen run set: the traces and metric blocks supplied for rr_q2, rr_q4 and stcf, the arrival/burst list (0,8), (0,8), (0,8), (2,1), (0,8), and the modelling conventions stated in the question (single processor, one CPU burst, no I/O, free initial dispatch, free same-process continuation, half-open intervals, arrivals before a slice end queued first, arrivals during switching appended to the tail, waiver only after an early finish). An assumption, not a fact, is that these burst lengths describe a real workload; they are exercise inputs. Likewise, the recommendation is relative to the stated objective and constraint, not a property of RR or STCF in general.

Why response and turnaround come apart. Response isolates access to the processor; turnaround adds everything after that access. Under Round Robin a job is guaranteed to reach the CPU within roughly one rotation, which is why the shortest quantum (q=2) has the smallest mean response (28/5). The same rotation then repeats, so completion can be postponed many rounds later: P1 starts at 0 but finishes at 39 under q=2, versus 9 under stcf. Under stcf the run-to-completion order is chosen by remaining service, so the late-arriving short job P4 preempts at t=2 and finishes at 3, giving the best mean turnaround (17), the fewest transitions (5), zero overhead and the smallest makespan (33) - while P5 waits until 25, which is why stcf has the worst mean response (51/5).

Why the two RR scenarios have exactly one free transition each. The waiver condition given in the question is an early completion in a run slice strictly shorter than a full quantum. P4 (burst 1) always completes inside such a slice, so the next different-process transition is waived exactly once per scenario: overhead = transitions - 1, i.e. 16 - 1 = 15 and 8 - 1 = 7. That arithmetic is consistent with makespan = 33 + overhead (48 and 40) and with switch_count counting the waived adjacent transition as well.

Why the constrained answer is what it is. Filtering first and optimizing second is the order the question requires: rr_q2 is excluded on overhead (15 > 8) even though its mean response is the smallest of the three, so the comparison that decides the recommendation is rr_q4 (48/5) against stcf (51/5). Their gap is 3/5, and it decomposes into per-process response differences of 0, +4, +7, -18, +10 (stcf minus rr_q4) - a narrow aggregate margin produced by large offsetting differences, not by uniform superiority. Two sensitivity statements keep the claim honest: a looser switching budget admits rr_q2 and changes the winner, and a turnaround- or makespan-based objective selects stcf. Both are hypothetical variations on the same frozen traces, not new simulations.

The source support used here is the supplied fixture on CPU scheduling (response and turnaround definitions, RR slice/context-switch tradeoff, the statement that neither a smaller average response nor a smaller switching fraction alone establishes the best policy, and that exercise burst lengths and budgets are not measured workload traces). No other sources are cited, and no number in the original question or tool output has been altered.

sections.heading: Scheduling metrics and conventions
sections.text: Processes are independent, have a single CPU burst and no I/O, on one processor with integer abstract time units. The listed burst lengths are known inputs supplied for this exercise, not predictions of a real workload. A completed process stops immediately without consuming the unused part of its quantum; any waiver of the following switching cost is a separate scenario rule. Simultaneous arrivals use lexicographic process ID order. Initial dispatch, dispatch after idle, and same-process continuation are free. Response time = first start − arrival; turnaround time = completion − arrival. Makespan is final completion measured from t=0, including all idle and switching time. Switch count includes adjacent different-process transitions, even free transitions, and excludes initial/after-idle dispatch. Timeline intervals are half-open [start, end); consecutive same-process runs are merged unless separated by switching or idle.

expected_steps: Order execution and switching intervals using the stated rules.
Compute process metrics and exact averages from first starts and completions.
Check service conservation and the requested state or constraint judgments.

All numbers below are read from the supplied deterministic runs; nothing is re-simulated.

1) Definitions and the response/turnaround split. Response time = first start - arrival; turnaround time = completion - arrival. Response records only when a process first gets the processor; turnaround additionally contains every later wait, preemption and switching delay. Frozen evidence: P1 first starts at t=0 (response 0) in all three scenarios, yet its turnaround is 39 (rr_q2), 25 (rr_q4) and 9 (stcf). Same response, very different completion - early access does not imply early completion. Within one scenario the same contrast appears: P4 in rr_q2 has response 10 (first start 12, arrival 2) but turnaround 11 (completion 13), because its first start and its completion are separated by service and (for longer jobs) by repeated requeueing. Turnaround can never be smaller than response for the same process.

2) Per-process first run and completion, and the averages they drive. rr_q2: first starts 0, 3, 6, 12, 9 and completions 39, 42, 45, 13, 48 for P1..P5, so mean response = 28/5 and mean turnaround = 37. stcf: first starts 0, 9, 17, 2, 25 and completions 9, 17, 25, 3, 33, so mean response = 51/5 and mean turnaround = 17. (For completeness rr_q4: first starts 0, 5, 10, 20, 15; completions 25, 30, 35, 21, 40; mean response 48/5; mean turnaround 149/5.) Total service is 33 units in every scenario and idle time is 0, so makespan = 33 + total switching overhead: 48, 40 and 33 respectively - a conservation check that the traces satisfy.

3) Where the rankings diverge. Mean response favours rr_q2 (28/5 = 5.6) over rr_q4 (48/5 = 9.6) over stcf (51/5 = 10.2). Mean turnaround reverses almost completely: stcf 17, then rr_q4 149/5 = 29.8, then rr_q2 37. Switch count and overhead: stcf 5 switches / 0 overhead, rr_q4 8 / 7, rr_q2 16 / 15. Makespan: stcf 33, rr_q4 40, rr_q2 48. So the mean-response winner (rr_q2) is last on turnaround, switches and makespan, while stcf is first on three metrics but last on mean response. rr_q4 is never first, but is second on both response and turnaround. Concretely, stcf beats rr_q4 on mean response components only for the short job: P4's response is 0 under stcf versus 18 under rr_q4 (18 units better), while P3 is 7 units worse and P5 10 units worse; the per-process differences sum to 3, exactly the 3/5 gap in the means (51/5 - 48/5 = 3/5).

4) Slice length and switching overhead (q=2 vs q=4). Doubling the quantum halves the transitions, 16 to 8, and cuts overhead from 15 to 7, but mean response worsens from 28/5 to 48/5 (a rise of 4 units). The overhead is not simply half of the switch count twice over because each RR scenario has exactly one waived transition: P4 completes inside a run slice of length 1, strictly shorter than the full quantum (1 < 2 and 1 < 4), so the following P4 -> P1 transition is free, giving 16 - 1 = 15 and 8 - 1 = 7. Slice-boundary behaviour is visible too: P4 arrives exactly at t=2, the end of P1's first q=2 slice. The stated rule enqueues that arrival before requeueing the unfinished P1, producing the first-rotation order P2, P3, P5, P4, then P1 - the order the trace shows (P4 runs at 12, P1 at 13). Under q=4, P4 arrives during P1's slice [0,4) and is queued at arrival; the same relative position results, but P4's first start slips from 12 to 20 (response 10 to 18). The t=0 tie among the four equal-burst jobs is settled by the stated lexicographic ID rule in both RR queue order and, in stcf, by smallest (remaining service, ID).

5) Constraint, objective and recommendation. Constraint total switching overhead <= 8: rr_q2 has 15 (violates), rr_q4 has 7 (satisfies), stcf has 0 (satisfies). Feasible set = {rr_q4, stcf}. Objective min mean response: rr_q4 = 48/5 = 9.6 versus stcf = 51/5 = 10.2, margin 3/5. Recommendation: rr_q4, and it is the unique optimum - no tie. The choice is genuinely constraint-driven: if the budget were looser (for example overhead <= 15 or at most 16 switches), rr_q2 would become feasible and would then minimize mean response at 28/5; if the objective were mean turnaround or makespan instead of mean response, stcf would win (17 < 149/5 < 37; 33 < 40 < 48).

6) Scope. Facts: for this five-process instance with the burst lengths given as inputs, and under the stated free initial dispatch, free same-process continuation, half-open intervals, boundary-queueing and early-finish waiver rules, q=4 Round Robin is the feasible mean-response minimum and the three metrics rank as shown. Not established: that q=4, Round Robin or STCF is optimal for other workloads, other quantum values, or other objectives. A single trace family cannot support a universal policy claim, and a lower mean response or a lower switching fraction by itself does not decide which policy is best.

Comparing the four listed metrics in the lower-is-better direction reveals a real tradeoff among these candidates: rr_q2 has lower mean response time than rr_q4 (28/5 < 48/5), but higher total switching overhead (15 > 7). Evaluate the stated constraints and objective together rather than selecting on one metric alone.
This conclusion applies only to the supplied workload, finite candidates, objective and constraints. Lower mean response or lower switching overhead alone does not establish a universally optimal policy or quantum.

Further analysis:
Reading the supplement (audit notes).

What is fact and what is assumption. Everything in the answer is a fact about this frozen run set: the traces and metric blocks supplied for rr_q2, rr_q4 and stcf, the arrival/burst list (0,8), (0,8), (0,8), (2,1), (0,8), and the modelling conventions stated in the question (single processor, one CPU burst, no I/O, free initial dispatch, free same-process continuation, half-open intervals, arrivals before a slice end queued first, arrivals during switching appended to the tail, waiver only after an early finish). An assumption, not a fact, is that these burst lengths describe a real workload; they are exercise inputs. Likewise, the recommendation is relative to the stated objective and constraint, not a property of RR or STCF in general.

Why response and turnaround come apart. Response isolates access to the processor; turnaround adds everything after that access. Under Round Robin a job is guaranteed to reach the CPU within roughly one rotation, which is why the shortest quantum (q=2) has the smallest mean response (28/5). The same rotation then repeats, so completion can be postponed many rounds later: P1 starts at 0 but finishes at 39 under q=2, versus 9 under stcf. Under stcf the run-to-completion order is chosen by remaining service, so the late-arriving short job P4 preempts at t=2 and finishes at 3, giving the best mean turnaround (17), the fewest transitions (5), zero overhead and the smallest makespan (33) - while P5 waits until 25, which is why stcf has the worst mean response (51/5).

Why the two RR scenarios have exactly one free transition each. The waiver condition given in the question is an early completion in a run slice strictly shorter than a full quantum. P4 (burst 1) always completes inside such a slice, so the next different-process transition is waived exactly once per scenario: overhead = transitions - 1, i.e. 16 - 1 = 15 and 8 - 1 = 7. That arithmetic is consistent with makespan = 33 + overhead (48 and 40) and with switch_count counting the waived adjacent transition as well.

Why the constrained answer is what it is. Filtering first and optimizing second is the order the question requires: rr_q2 is excluded on overhead (15 > 8) even though its mean response is the smallest of the three, so the comparison that decides the recommendation is rr_q4 (48/5) against stcf (51/5). Their gap is 3/5, and it decomposes into per-process response differences of 0, +4, +7, -18, +10 (stcf minus rr_q4) - a narrow aggregate margin produced by large offsetting differences, not by uniform superiority. Two sensitivity statements keep the claim honest: a looser switching budget admits rr_q2 and changes the winner, and a turnaround- or makespan-based objective selects stcf. Both are hypothetical variations on the same frozen traces, not new simulations.

sources.text:
A scheduler chooses which ready job receives the processor. Turnaround time equals completion time minus arrival time. Response time equals the first time a job runs minus its arrival time. These metrics measure different things: early access to a processor does not necessarily imply early completion. First-come, first-served runs jobs in arrival order without preempting them. Shortest Job First selects the shortest available job and is non-preemptive. Shortest Time-to-Completion First is preemptive and selects the job with the least remaining processing time. Comparisons involving these shortest-job policies must state how execution lengths are known.

Round Robin rotates through a ready queue, running each selected job for at most one time slice before moving an unfinished job to the back. Shorter slices can improve initial responsiveness but increase the frequency of context switches. Larger slices amortize switching costs but can lengthen waits before a different job first runs. Neither a smaller average response time nor a smaller switching fraction alone establishes that a policy is best for every objective.

A multi-level feedback queue, or MLFQ, uses observed execution behavior instead of requiring exact future job lengths. Jobs in higher-priority queues run before lower-priority jobs; equal-priority jobs can share service by Round Robin. New jobs begin at high priority, and consuming the allowed CPU allotment causes demotion. Accounting for total consumed allotment prevents a job from retaining high priority indefinitely merely by yielding just before each slice ends. Periodic priority boosts can help jobs otherwise left waiting at low priority. Queue levels, slice lengths, allotments, and boost intervals are policy parameters, not universal constants.

This fixture adds an explicit scheduling model for exercises. It is authored example scaffolding rather than text copied from a textbook. Unless a question states otherwise, there is one processor, jobs are independent, and each job consists of one CPU burst with no I/O. Arrival times and required CPU service are provided. The processor never serves two jobs simultaneously. Time spent switching is not CPU service delivered to any job. A job that finishes before its slice ends does not use the remaining slice. If a job arrives at exactly a slice boundary, the question must say whether that arrival is enqueued before or after the preempted job. Ties must be resolved by an explicit rule, such as alphabetical job names.

A question that includes switching overhead must define when that overhead applies: for example, only when moving between different jobs, with no initial dispatch charge. It must also state whether arrivals can occur while switching and how they enter the queue. Questions that ignore overhead must say so. These conventions make a timeline reproducible and prevent a numeric answer from depending on unstated simulator behavior.

A comparison can report each job's first-run and completion times, then compute the requested averages. A design recommendation also needs an objective and constraints, such as a maximum response time, a switching budget, or a fairness requirement. A policy can satisfy one constraint while losing on another metric. Choosing a scheduler should therefore follow the stated workload and requirements. Hypothetical burst lengths and budgets introduced in an exercise are not measured workload traces, and labels assigned by the generator are not empirical student difficulty measurements.
